  - Origins in 1851; incorporated in New York in 1936; name changed from Corning Glass Works to Corning Incorporated in 1989.

  - Serves optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass applications.

  - Process is scalable and viewed as cost‑effective for producing large‑size substrates.

summary:
- Part of Corning Incorporated’s annual report (Part I, Item 1. Business) with a forward-looking statements caution referencing Risk Factors and MD&A.
- Company overview: origins in 1851; incorporated in NY in 1936; name changed to Corning Incorporated in 1989. Leader in materials science leveraging glass science, ceramic science, and optical physics; success driven by R&D, material/process innovation, and deep customer relationships.
- Markets served: optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass products.
- Representative products: damage-resistant cover glass; precision display glass; optical fiber, cable, wireless and connectivity solutions; life-sciences tools; and clean-air technologies.
- Operating structure: five reportable segments—Display Technologies, Optical Communications, Specialty Materials, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences; manufacturing at 119 plants in 15 countries.
- Display Technologies segment: produces glass substrates for LCD and OLED displays used in TVs, notebooks, monitors, tablets, and handheld devices; relies on Corning’s proprietary, highly automated fusion manufacturing process delivering pristine surfaces, thermal stability, dimensional uniformity, scalability, and cost-effectiveness.
- Recent display innovations: EAGLE XG Slim Glass (>35 billion square feet sold); Astra Glass for high-resolution/oxide backplanes; Lotus NXT Glass for high-temperature processing and flexible/small devices; first Gen 10/10.5 substrate sizes for large displays.
- Display footprint and IP: manufacturing in China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan; patent protection and trade secrets are important; segment was 26% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Optical Communications segment: Corning pioneered low-loss optical fiber (1970); addresses growing bandwidth demand and migration from copper to optical; delivers solutions across the network edge.
- Segment organization: carrier network (telecom infrastructure for video/data/voice) and enterprise network (optical networks for businesses, governments, individuals).
- Carrier network portfolio: broad fibers (Vascade for submarine; LEAF for long-haul/metro; SMF-28 ULL/TXF, SMF-28e+, ClearCurve, SMF-28 Ultra/Contour for various applications), sold directly and via third-party cablers; cable lines (RocketRibbon, miniXtend) for outdoor/indoor and 5G deployments.
- Connectivity and systems: hardware and equipment (assemblies, hardware, connectors, components, closures, network interface devices) offered as components or integrated solutions, including Evolv (pre-connectorized FTTH/5G) and Centrix (high-density fiber management).

summary:
- Overview of Corning’s business segments and product leadership, focusing on Display Technologies, Optical Communications, and Specialty Materials.
- Display Technologies: Positions Corning as a leader in precision glass for larger, thinner, flexible, high‑resolution displays; highlights key innovations (EAGLE XG Slim Glass, Astra Glass for oxide backplanes and LTPS processes, Lotus NXT for high‑temperature/small and flexible devices, and first Gen 10/10.5 substrate sizes for large displays). Notes manufacturing footprint across China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan; emphasizes patent/trade secret importance; segment accounted for 26% of 2021 net sales.
- Optical Communications: Traces heritage from inventing low‑loss optical fiber; addresses surging data/video demand driving shift from copper to fiber. Details carrier and enterprise product groupings:
  - Carrier network: Broad fiber portfolio (Vascade for submarine, LEAF for long‑haul/metro, SMF‑28 ULL/TXF, SMF‑28e+, ClearCurve, SMF‑28 Ultra/Contour), internal and external cabling (RocketRibbon, miniXtend) for outdoor/indoor and 5G; hardware/equipment (assemblies, connectors, closures, components) and integrated solutions (Evolv for pre‑connectorized FTTH/5G, Centrix for high‑density fiber management); includes select copper products (subscriber demarcation, xDSL passives, enclosures).
  - Enterprise network: ClearCurve multimode fiber for data centers; hardware/equipment; integrated solutions (EDGE platform for high‑density cabling to 400G+; Everon for indoor cellular connectivity).
  - Manufacturing footprint: Fiber in North Carolina, China, India (Poland added in 2022); cabling in North Carolina, Poland, regional sites; hardware/equipment in Texas, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Poland, China. Notes extensive patent portfolio and limited royalty income; segment represented 31% of 2021 net sales.
- Specialty Materials: Provides 150+ glass, glass‑ceramic, and crystal formulations plus precision metrology instruments/software for diverse markets (mobile electronics, semiconductor optics/consumables, aerospace/defense optics, radiation shielding, sunglasses, telecom components).
  - Gorilla Glass (including Gorilla Glass Victus) for enhanced drop/scratch resistance, optical clarity, touch sensitivity, RF transparency; manufactured in the U.S., South Korea, Taiwan.
  - Ceramic Shield: First transparent, color‑free glass‑ceramic for smartphones, co‑developed and scaled with Apple for iPhone front covers.
  - Semiconductor optics: HPFS Fused Silica, ULE Ultra‑Low Expansion Glass, metrology instruments, custom assemblies; manufactured in New York.
  - Ultra‑flat/ultra‑thin glass wafers/substrates for AR, advanced packaging, 3D sensing; made in New York, France, China.
  - Additional products: Tinted sunglasses and radiation shielding produced in France.
- Emphasis on intellectual property across segments, referencing a broader “Patents and Trademarks” section.

Optical Communications Segment
 
Corning invented the world’s firs
t low-loss optical fiber in 1970. Since that milestone, we have continued to pioneer optical fiber, cable and connectivity solutions. Asglobal demand driven by video usag
e grows exponentially, telecommunications networks continue to migrate from copper to optical-based systems that can deliver therequired cost-effe
ctive capacity. Our experience puts us in a unique position to design and deliver optical solutions that reach every edge of the communications network. 
This segment is divided into two m
ain product groupings – carrier network and enterprise network. The carrier network group consists primarily of products and solutionsfor optical-based com
munications infrastructure for services such as video, data and voice communications. The enterprise network group consists primarily of optical-basedcommunication networks sold to bus
inesses, governments and individuals for their own use. 
Our carrier network product po
rtfolio encompasses an array of optical fiber products, including Vascade® optical fibers for use in submarine networks; LEAF® optical fiberfor long-haul, regional and 
metropolitan networks; SMF-28® ULL and TXF® fiber for more scalable long-haul and regional networks; SMF-28e+™ single-mode opticalfiber providing additiona
l transmission wavelengths in metropolitan and access networks, and ClearCurve® ultra-bendable single-mode fiber for use in multiple-dwellingunits and fiber-to-the

ry-leading attenuation, compatibility, and improved macrobend performance in one fiber. A portion of our optical fiber is solddirectly to end users and th
ird-party cablers globally. Corning’s remaining fiber production is cabled internally and sold to end users as either bulk cable or as part of anintegrated optical so
lution. Corning’s cable products, including the RocketRibbon® and miniXtend® portfolios, support various outdoor, indoor/outdoor and indoorapplications and include 
a broad range of loose tube, ribbon and drop cable designs with flame-retardant versions available for indoor and indoor/outdoor use including 5Gnetworks.

Specialty Materials Segment
 
The Specialty Materia
ls segment manufactures products that provide more than 150 material formulations for glass, glass ceramics, and crystals, as well as precisionmetrology instruments and so
ftware to meet requirements for unique customer needs. Consequently, this segment operates in a wide variety of commercial and industrialmarkets including mat
erials optimized for mobile consumer electronics, semiconductor equipment optics and consumables, aerospace and defense optics, radiation shieldingproducts, sunglasses, and teleco
mmunications components. 
Our highly durable glass, known as Corning® Gorill
a® Glass, is a chemically strengthened thin glass designed specifically to function as a cover, or back-enclosure glass,for mobile consumer el
ectronic devices such as mobile phones, tablets, laptops and smartwatches. Elegant and lightweight, Corning® Gorilla® Glass is durable enough toresist many real-world 
events that commonly cause wear or scratch damage and glass failure, while providing optical clarity, touch sensitivity, and RF transparency, thusenabling exciting new appli
cations in technology and design. In 2020, Corning unveiled its toughest Gorilla Glass yet, Corning® Gorilla® Glass Victus®, whichsignificantly improves bo
th drop and scratch performance, addressing consumer demand for improved durability. Corning® Gorilla® Glass is manufactured in the UnitedStates ("U.S."), South Korea and Taiwan.
 
‎In 2020, Corning invented the world’s fi
rst transparent, color-free glass-ceramic suitable for smartphone applications, which is featured as "Ceramic Shield" on the frontcover of the latest iPhone 
models. Apple and Corning partnered to develop and scale the manufacturing of Ceramic Shield, which offers unparalleled durability andtoughness.
 
Corning’s semiconductor optics 
include high-performance optical materials including Corning® HPFS® Fused Silica and Corning® ULE® Ultra-Low Expansion Glass,optical-based metro
logy instruments, and custom optical assemblies for applications in the global semiconductor industry. Corning’s semiconductor optics products aremanufactured in New York.
 
Corning also manufactures ul
tra-flat, ultra-thin glass wafers and substrates for a variety of applications including augmented reality, advanced semiconductor packaging, 3Dsensing, and more. These products a
re manufactured in New York, France, and China.   
Other specialty glass produc
ts include tinted sunglasses and radiation shielding products that are made in France.

text:
Environmental Technologies Segment
 
Corning’s Environmental Technolog
ies segment manufactures ceramic substrates and filter products for emissions control in mobile applications around the world.  In theearly 1970s, Corning developed an econo
mical, high-performance cellular ceramic substrate that is now the standard for catalytic converters in vehicles worldwide.  Asglobal emissions control r
egulations tighten, Corning has continued to develop more effective and durable ceramic substrate and filter products for gasoline and dieselapplications, most rec
ently launching low-mass Corning® FLORA® substrates and Corning® DuraTrap® GC gasoline particulate filters. Corning manufactures substrateand filter products in New York, Virgin
ia, China, Germany and South Africa. Corning sells its ceramic substrate and filter products worldwide to catalyzers andmanufacturers of em
ission control systems who then sell to automotive and diesel vehicle or engine manufacturers.  Although most sales are made to the emission controlsystems manufacturers, 
the use of Corning substrates and filters is generally required by the specifications of the automotive and diesel vehicle or engine manufacturers.

rtant to the segment’s operations. The segment has an extensive portfolio of patents relating to its products, technologies and manufacturingprocesses. Corning is licensed to us
e certain patents owned by others, which are also considered important to the segment’s operations. Refer to the material under theheading “Patents and Tradem
arks” for information relating to the Company’s patents and trademarks. 
The Environmental Technologi
es segment represented 11% of Corning’s consolidated net sales in 2021.

ains within our leadership teams.  Since 2010, gender and ethnic diversity among members of the Corporate Management Group, which includes about230 of the Company’s top global lead
ers, increased from 28% to 50%; corporate officer diverse representation has increased from 21% to 38%.  
In 2021, as planned, we achieved 100% pay 
equity for all salaried men and women in our worldwide operations and we continued to maintain pay equity across minoritygroups compared with white sala
ried employees in the U.S. We furthered our longstanding commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion in 2020 by creating the Office ofRacial Equality and Social Uni
ty (ORESU) to further our goal of a more equitable and inclusive culture at Corning and beyond. The efforts of this office have not onlyimpacted policies, pr
actices, communications, and our corporate culture, but have championed diversity and inclusion in the communities in which our employees live andwork.  Since its creation, in add
ition to launching enterprise-wide Unconscious Bias training and entering a $5.5 million strategic partnership with North Carolina A&TUniversity, ORESU is also engaging with local co
mmunities to enhance public safety and create places where students of color can thrive. 
Corning proudly sponsors 16 different Emp
loyee Resource Groups ("ERGs") with 59 chapters worldwide. They represent employees who are women, Black, Asian, Latino,Native American, people with d
isabilities, members of the LGBTQ+ community, and veterans, among others. The ERGs are vital in raising awareness, recruiting andretaining diverse ta
lent, and inspiring corporate leadership to adopt new policies, practices, and services.

title: Talent Management
heading: Talent Management
start_phrase:
Each year we formally ev
aluate the talent implications of our strategic business plans and align our actions and objectives accordingly.
summary:
- Human Capital Management Overview: Corning’s talent strategy to attract, retain, and develop employees to support innovation and long careers; global footprint of 61,200 employees in 44 countries; workforce concentration in North America, Asia Pacific, and EMEA; 68% in production/maintenance roles; about 66% covered by unions or works councils.

- Values: Company’s seven core Values (Quality, Integrity, Performance, Leadership, Innovation, Independence, and the Individual); emphasis on “how” work is done; annual Corporate Values Survey to measure and improve adherence.

- Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: Workforce gender mix (61% men, 39% women); initiatives to build pipelines for women and underrepresented talent through recruitment, mentoring, coaching, networking, and development; leadership diversity gains since 2010 (Corporate Management Group diverse representation from 28% to 50%; corporate officer diversity from 21% to 38%); 2021 achievement of 100% pay equity for salaried men and women globally and maintained pay equity for U.S. minority groups; creation of the Office of Racial Equality and Social Unity (ORESU) in 2020, enterprise-wide Unconscious Bias training, $5.5M partnership with North Carolina A&T, and community engagement; support for 16 Employee Resource Groups with 59 chapters representing multiple affinity groups.

- Talent Management: Alignment of talent plans with business strategy and growth (including acquisitions); net addition of ~11,100 employees in 2021; strategic pipelines via internships, co-ops, rotational programs, and partnerships with universities (including HBCUs) and professional organizations (e.g., SWE, ALPFA, NSBE, NABA, Out for Undergrad, veterans’ groups); regular climate and pulse surveys; comprehensive development offerings (digital/classroom/blended), on-the-job learning, mentoring, and career planning; strong historical retention with targeted responses to 2021 U.S. challenges; 2021 salaried retention at 94%.

- Health, Safety, and Wellbeing: Standards meeting/exceeding regulations; top-quartile safety performance in ORCHSE peer group; 2021 total recordable incident rate (TRIR) of 0.50; regional wellness programs (nutrition, mental health, fitness, smoking cessation, smoke-free campuses); continued COVID-19 measures via the Responsible Corning program; promotion of vaccinations and delivery of 100,000+ vaccine doses to employees, families, and communities in locations including Reynosa (Mexico), Asan (Korea), and Pune (India).

- Executive Officers of the Registrant: Profiles and roles of several senior leaders, including John P. Bayne, Jr. (Mobile Consumer Electronics), Stefan Becker (Operations Controller), Michael A. Bell (Optical Communications), Cheryl C. Capps (Chief Supply Chain Officer), Martin J. Curran (Innovation Officer), Jeffrey W. Evenson (Chief Strategy Officer), and Li Fang (Greater China), highlighting tenure, career progression, and current responsibilities.

Talent Management
 
Each year we formally ev
aluate the talent implications of our strategic business plans and align our actions and objectives accordingly.  As businesses grow organically orthrough acquisition, we crea
te human capital objectives to ensure we have the right people with the right skills in place to deliver that growth.  In 2021, as a result of theseobjectives, our talent p
rocesses supported the net addition of approximately 11,100 employees worldwide, with significant growth in all regions.

 attract and recruit diverse qualified candidates to maintain our culture of innovation and to foster creativity.  We have created a strategic talent pipelinethrough internships, co-opera
tives, rotational leadership programs, and partnerships with various universities, including Historically Black Colleges & Universities(HBCUs).  In addition, we collaborate with o
rganizations such as the Society of Women Engineers, The Association of Latino Professionals for America, National Societyof Black Engineers, National Associ
ation of Black Accountants, Out for Undergrad, and military veterans’ groups to introduce us to qualified, diverse candidates. 
Businesses conduct climate su
rveys at least every two years, and ad hoc pulse surveys as needed, to measure engagement, satisfaction and alignment with our Values.  It isimportant to Corning that e
mployees develop, grow and are inspired to continue their careers at the Company over the long-term.  We offer rich simulations, assessments,and experiences that a
re digital, classroom, and a blend of both, targeted to all levels in the organization.  We provide on-the-job learning experience, mentoring, and careerplanning to ensure immedi
ate application and lasting impact.  Talent retention is an ongoing important focus area which aligns with our strategy of encouraging andsupporting longer-term c
areers with Corning.  Historically, our talent retention has been consistently higher than the markets in which we compete for talent.  Although 2021yielded some recruit
ment and retention challenges primarily in specific locations within our US operations, our talent management approach enabled our HR teams tomobilize quickly with plans 
in place to address those issues.  Salaried talent retention in 2021 was 94%. 
At Corning, the health and safety o
f our workforce is always of paramount consideration.  Our safety standards always meet, and often exceed, local regulatory standards. We continue to rank within th
e top quartile of our ORCHSE Strategies, LLC. (a National Safety Council membership-based workplace safety group) peer group in termsof total recordable 
incident rate (TRIR) performance with a Company-wide TRIR of just 0.50 in 2021.  We promote employee wellbeing through wellness programs whichvary by region such as nutrition, 
mental health, and fitness-related offerings, smoking cessation programs, and smoke free campuses. With the continuation of the pandemicin 2021, we continued our Responsible Corning progr
am with enhanced cleaning, screening, testing and other measures initiated in 2020. In addition, we encouragedCOVID vaccinations and boosters among our e
mployees and in the communities in which we operate, supplying more than 100,000 vaccines to employees, families andcommunity members in lo

summary:
- Excerpt from Item 1A. Risk Factors outlining that the company (Corning) operates in rapidly changing economic, political, and technological environments, with risks that could affect operations, financial results, cash flows, strategy execution, and the trading price of its securities. The section complements MD&A and the financial statements and is not exhaustive; risks may cause future results to differ from forward-looking statements and historical trends.

- COVID-19-related risks: ongoing and potentially renewed pandemic impacts on the global economy, financial and capital markets, exchange and interest rates, and on the company’s workforce, operations, suppliers, contract manufacturers, and customers due to measures like travel restrictions, quarantines, mandates, and shutdowns; significant uncertainty around duration, scope, and severity; potential adverse effects on results of operations.

- Inflation and input availability: rising prices and uncertain availability of commodities, raw materials, utilities, labor, and logistics could increase production and shipping costs, disrupt timely supply, and pressure margins. Passing cost increases to customers may reduce demand, delay or cancel orders, and negatively affect operating results, profitability, and strategy execution.

- Supply chain, manufacturing, and demand-forecast risks: disruptions, delays, transportation interruptions, and shortages of materials, equipment, and services (some with long lead times or single/limited-source suppliers) can hinder meeting customer demand, raise costs, and create excess or obsolete inventory. Volatile demand for manufacturing equipment heightens capital and operational risks across the supply chain and may lead suppliers to exit or scale back, further impairing the ability to secure necessary inputs (including raw/batch materials, natural resources, and utilities) and negatively impacting the business.

Risk Factors section outlining material risks that could affect Corning’s business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, ability to execute strategy, and the trading price of its securities. The discussion is complementary to MD&A and the consolidated financial statements and includes forward-looking cautionary language.

- Macroeconomic and public health risk:
  - Ongoing COVID-19 impacts on global economic activity, financial and capital markets, FX and interest rates, and on Corning’s workforce, operations, customers, suppliers, and contract manufacturers. Significant uncertainty remains around duration, scope, and severity.

- Inflation and input cost risk:
  - Inflationary pressures and uncertain availability of commodities, raw materials, utilities, labor, and logistics capacity can increase production and shipping costs, disrupt supply, and pressure profitability. Passing cost increases to customers may reduce demand and adversely affect results and strategy execution.

- Supply chain, operations, and forecasting risks:
  - Dependence on timely supply of equipment, raw and batch materials, natural resources, utilities, and services; exposure to single- or limited-source suppliers and long lead times.
  - Potential manufacturing interruptions, delivery delays, higher costs, or order cancellations due to:
    - Inaccurate demand forecasting; scarcity and price volatility of materials and services.
    - Import/export approval challenges and transportation delays/capacity constraints.
    - Global semiconductor component shortages.
    - IT or infrastructure failures (including third-party providers).
    - Natural disasters, climate change effects and extreme weather, utility interruptions, epidemics/pandemics, geopolitical turmoil, increased U.S.–China and other trade restrictions, social unrest, political instability, terrorism, or acts of war in locations important to Corning or its customers/suppliers.
  - Industry demand volatility can prompt suppliers to scale back/exit, impairing Corning’s ability to meet customer demand.

- Segment concentration risk:
  - Heavy reliance on the Display Technologies segment for profits and cash flow; ongoing display glass pricing pressure from competition, potential over-capacity, and new technologies. Failure to reduce costs or increase volumes proportionately could materially harm financial results.

- Customer concentration risk:
  - A small number of end customers account for a high share of sales, creating exposure to:
    - Loss or insolvency of key customers and resulting cash flow impacts.
    - Customer leverage in contractual negotiations.
    - Further concentration through customer mergers and consolidations.

mental liabilities related to property owned by Corning based on expert analysis and continual monitoring by both internal and externalconsultants. At December 31, 2021 and 2020, Corning h

ibuting to sales and earnings growth and strong free cash flow in the second half of 2020 and full year 2021.

ll continue to use its cash to grow, extend its leadership and reward shareholders.  Our key growth drivers remain intact, and some areaccelerating as key

title: CORE PERFORMANCE MEASURES - Introduction
heading: CORE PERFORMANCE MEASURES
start_phrase:
In managing the Company and assessing ou
r financial performance, we adjust certain measures provided by our consolidated financial statements to exclude specific itemsto report core perfor
mance measures.
summary: Corning’s Core Performance Measures adjust GAAP results to exclude items not reflective of ongoing operations—such as gains/losses on translated earnings contracts, acquisition-related costs, discrete tax items and other tax adjustments, restructuring, impairment losses, other charges/credits, certain litigation expenses, and pension mark-to-market adjustments—across the Company and equity affiliates. The company employs constant-currency reporting for Display Technologies, Environmental Technologies, Specialty Materials, and Life Sciences, using the Japanese yen, South Korean won, Chinese yuan, new Taiwan dollar, and euro, to reduce currency volatility and reflect the economics of translated earnings contracts. These non-GAAP measures are intended to better indicate core operating performance and align with management’s decision-making, but are not a substitute for GAAP. Corning cannot provide GAAP outlooks or reconcile forward-looking non-GAAP measures due to the inability to forecast currency movements and other non-operational or uncontrollable items. Reconciliations to the closest GAAP measures are provided in “Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures.”
text:
CORE PERFORMANCE MEASURES
 
In managing the Company and assessing ou
r financial performance, we adjust certain measures provided by our consolidated financial statements to exclude specific itemsto report core perfor
mance measures. These items include gains and losses on our translated earnings contracts, acquisition-related costs, certain discrete tax items and othertax-related adjustments, restruct
uring, impairment losses, and other charges and credits, certain litigation-related expenses, pension mark-to-market adjustments and otheritems which do not reflec
t on-going operating results of the Company or our equity affiliates. Corning utilizes constant-currency reporting for our Display Technologies,Environmental Technologies, Spe
cialty Materials and Life Sciences segments for the Japanese yen, South Korean won, Chinese yuan, new Taiwan dollar and the euro.  TheCompany believes that the use o
f constant-currency reporting allows investors to understand our results without the volatility of currency fluctuations and reflects theunderlying economics of the 
translated earnings contracts used to mitigate the impact of changes in currency exchange rates on our earnings and cash flows. Corning alsobelieves that reporting core
 performance measures provides investors greater transparency to the information used by our management team to make financial andoperational decisions.
 
Core performance measu
res are not prepared in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles in the U.S. (“GAAP”). We believe investors should considerthese non-GAAP measures in evaluating ou
r results as they are more indicative of our core operating performance and how management evaluates our operational resultsand trends. These measures a
re not, and should not be viewed as a substitute for, GAAP reporting measures. With respect to the Company’s outlook for future periods, it isnot possible to provide reconc
iliations for these non-GAAP measures because the Company does not forecast the movement of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar, orother items that do not r
eflect ongoing operations, nor does it forecast items that have not yet occurred or a
re out of the Company’s control. As a result, the Company is unable to provide outlook information on a GAAP basis. 
For a reconciliation of non
-GAAP performance measures to their most directly comparable GAAP financial measure, please see “Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Measures”.

ain financial measures and key performance indicators that are not calculated in accordance with GAAP to assess our financial and operating performance.

title: Items Excluded from GAAP Measures
heading: Items Excluded from GAAP Measures
start_phrase:
Items we exclude from GAAP measures 
to arrive at core performance measures are as follows:
summary:
- Overview of non-GAAP adjustments used to derive core performance measures, with rationale and scope.
- Constant-currency methodology: justification due to multi-currency revenues/expenses; impacted segments and currencies; management-set hedge-aligned rates (JPY 107, KRW 1,175, CNY 6.7, TWD 31, EUR 0.81).
- Specific exclusions from GAAP to core measures:
  - Translation gains/losses on JPY-denominated debt.
  - Gains/losses on translated earnings hedges (JPY, KRW, CNY, EUR, TWD; GBP unrealized).
  - Acquisition-related costs (intangible amortization, inventory step-up, deal costs).
  - Discrete tax items and other tax adjustments (law changes, audits, reserves, DTA realizability, Subpart F, etc.).
  - Pension mark-to-market adjustments.
  - Restructuring, impairment, other charges/credits (including accelerated depreciation, asset write-offs, 3Q21 power-outage repair costs with expected insurance recoveries).
  - Litigation, regulatory, and other legal matters (including environmental liabilities).
  - Preferred stock conversion (put option under Share Repurchase Agreement with Samsung Display Co., Ltd.).
  - Bond redemption loss (debenture redemption premiums).
  - (Loss) gain on investments (mark-to-market/fair value changes or dispositions).
  - Gain on sale of businesses.
  - Equity in losses of affiliates (non-continuing ops costs like restructuring, impairments, inventory, take-or-pay settlements; 2020 loss tied to a business sale).
  - Transaction-related gain (previously held equity in HSG).
  - Cumulative $105M revenue reduction in 1Q20 for a customer contract after exit from LCD panel production.
- Reportable segments defined:
  - Display Technologies (LCD and advanced display glass).
  - Optical Communications (carrier and enterprise network components).
  - Specialty Materials (glass/ceramics/crystals across 150+ formulations).
  - Environmental Technologies (ceramic substrates/filters for auto/diesel).
  - Life Sciences (labware, equipment, media, serum, reagents for discovery/bioproduction).
  - “All Other” includes HSG, pharmaceutical technologies, auto glass, new product lines/projects, other businesses, and certain corporate investments; HSG consolidated since Sep 9, 2020.
- Segment reporting approach:
  - Prepared consistent with internal CODM view.
  - Segment sales and net income exclude specified currency impacts (Display & Specialty: JPY/KRW/CNY/TWD; Environmental: EUR/CNY; Life Sciences: EUR/CNY/JPY).
  - Unallocated items (hedge impacts, acquisition costs, discrete taxes, legal matters, restructuring/impairment, acquisition adjustments, and other non-recurring/non-operational items) excluded from segment results but included in consolidated results.
  - Equity affiliates’ earnings tied to segments included in segment results; allocations may differ from stand-alone; comparability to other companies may vary.
- Display Technologies segment performance:
  - Net sales: $3,700M (2021), $3,172M (2020), $3,254M (2019); +17% YoY in 2021 driven by mid-teens volume growth with stable pricing.
  - Segment net income: $960M (2021), $717M (2020), $786M (2019); +34% YoY in 2021 primarily from higher sales.
text:
Items Excluded from GAAP Measures
 
Items we exclude from GAAP measures 
to arrive at core performance measures are as follows: 
(1)
Constant-currency adjustment:  Because a significant po rtion of segment revenue and expenses are denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar,management believes 
it is important to understand the impact on core net income of translating these currencies into U.S. dollars.  Our Display Technologies andSpecialty Materials s
egments sales and net income are primarily denominated in Japanese yen, but are also impacted by the South Korean won, Chinese yuan, andnew Taiwan dollar.  Environmenta
l Technologies and Life Science segment sales and net income are primarily impacted by the euro and Chinese yuan.  Presentingresults on a constant-c
urrency basis mitigates the translation impact and allows management to evaluate performance period over period, analyze underlying trendsin our businesses, and establish ope
rational goals and forecasts.  We establish constant-currency rates based on internally derived management estimates which areclosely aligned with the cu

title: Management Assessment of Liquidity
heading: Management Assessment of Liquidity
start_phrase: We ended 2021 with $2.1 billion of cash and cash equivalents.
summary:
- Cash flows: In 2021, operating cash flow increased by $1.232 billion driven by higher net income; investing cash outflows rose $109 million on higher capital expenditures; financing cash outflows rose $1.723 billion, mainly from higher debt repayments ($639 million), redemption of Preferred Stock ($507 million), and cash paid for share repurchases ($169 million).

- Defined benefit pension plans: Corning’s U.S. qualified plan represents 77% of projected benefit obligation and 86% of plan assets. In 2021, no voluntary contributions were made to the U.S. plan; $24 million was contributed to international plans. Expected 2022 contributions to international plans are $29 million.

- Balance sheet and working capital (12/31/21 vs. 12/31/20): Working capital decreased to $2.853 billion (from $4.237 billion) and current ratio to 1.6x (from 2.1x). Trade receivables declined to $2.004 billion with DSO improving to 49 days (from 57). Inventories rose to $2.481 billion with turns improving to 3.7x (from 3.2x). DPO increased to 50 days (from 44). Long-term debt fell to $6.989 billion and total debt to $7.044 billion; total debt-to-capital improved to 36% (from 37%).

- Liquidity and capital resources: Year-end cash and equivalents were $2.1 billion, about 58% held outside the U.S., generally unrestricted. A $1.5 billion commercial paper program and a $1.5 billion revolving credit facility were both undrawn at year-end. The company expects operating cash flow, existing cash, and potential debt issuance to fund near-term needs and states sufficient liquidity for at least the next 12 months. Leverage covenant (max 60%) under the revolver stood at ~36% at year-end; in compliance with all covenants and default provisions; no known trends likely to materially reduce liquidity.

- Share repurchases: Open-market repurchases totaled 7.3 million shares for ~$274 million in 2021 (4.1 million shares for ~$105 million in 2020). On April 8, 2021, the company repurchased 35 million shares for ~$1.5 billion following Preferred Stock conversion, with $507 million paid at closing and additional $507 million payments due on each of the first and second anniversaries.

- Customer credit and receivables: Ongoing monitoring of significant customers; accounts receivable sales of $602 million in 2021, of which $405 million was expected to be collected in the normal course. No material liquidity impact identified from customer credit issues.

- Foreign currency hedging (translated earnings): Substantial hedging of Japanese yen exposure for 2022–2024 using forwards and options; 2021 pre-tax net gain of $363 million (including $27 million realized), versus a 2020 pre-tax net loss of $38 million (including $31 million realized); notional outstanding $6.5 billion. Korean won exposure hedged with average rate forwards; 2021 pre-tax net loss of $33 million (including $11 million realized) versus a 2020 pre-tax net gain of $24 million (including $1 million realized); notional outstanding $1.2 billion in 2021 ($0.4 billion in 2020).

title: Valuation of the Previously Held Equity Interest from the Consolidation of HSG
heading: Valuation of the Previously Held Equity Interes t from the Consolidation of HSG
start_phrase: We account for the chang e in controlling interest using the acquisition method of accounting, which requires us to estimate the fair values of the assets and liabilities recorded.
summary:
- Consolidation of HSG and acquisition accounting: change in controlling interest accounted for using the acquisition method, requiring fair value measurements of acquired assets (intangible assets like developed technologies/know-how, tradenames, customer-related intangibles; fixed assets; inventories) and assumed liabilities (customer deposits, deferred revenue, debt, other liabilities). Independent appraisals and valuation models used; allocation period up to one year may adjust recorded values with offsetting goodwill changes; estimate changes can impact future financial results.
- Remeasurement gain on previously held equity interest: following HSG’s September 2020 redemption of DuPont’s stake for $250 million, Corning recognized a $498 million pre-tax gain from remeasuring its equity method investment to fair value, determined via an income approach using projected revenue, a 16.5% discount rate, and 0% terminal growth.
- Recognition and valuation of intangible assets: at consolidation, Corning recorded $215 million of developed technologies and know-how and $70 million of other intangibles, amortized over approximately 20 and 15 years, respectively. Developed technologies and know-how were valued using (1) relief-from-royalty method for $125 million (21.0% discount rate, 7.0% royalty rate) and (2) multi-period excess earnings method for $90 million (19.0% discount rate).
- Valuation of customer deposits and deferred revenue: recorded a $264 million customer deposit liability at fair value related to refundable payments under a long-term supply agreement (discount rates 2.54%–3.23%; expected repayment 2029–2034 contingent on purchase obligations). Recorded $1,070 million of deferred revenue at fair value for non-refundable consideration under long-term supply agreements, valued using a cost approach (bottom-up cost buildup) reflecting costs to fulfill and a normal profit margin.
- References to additional disclosures: Note 3 (Investments) and Note 4 (HSG Transactions and Acquisitions).
- Impairment of long-lived assets: policy requires assessing recoverability when indicators are present and performing quarterly reviews when indicators exist, involving significant judgment.

title: Impairment of assets held for use
heading: Impairment of assets held for use
start_phrase: We are required to ass ess the recoverability of the carrying value of long-lived assets when an indicator of impairment has been identified.
summary:
- Consolidation of HSG and remeasurement: Corning applied the acquisition method to a change in control of HSG, fair-valuing acquired assets (including intangibles, fixed assets, inventories) and liabilities (debt, customer deposits, deferred revenue). Previously held equity interest was remeasured to fair value with resulting gain recognized. Independent appraisals and acceptable valuation models were used; allocation-period adjustments (up to one year) may change values and goodwill.

- September 2020 Redemption details: HSG redeemed DuPont’s interest for $250 million, triggering consolidation and a $498 million pre-tax gain on Corning’s previously held equity method investment, valued via an income approach (16.5% discount rate, 0% terminal growth).

- Intangible assets recognized: $215 million for developed technologies/know-how and $70 million for other intangibles, amortized over ~20 and ~15 years, respectively. Valuation methods included relief-from-royalty ($125 million; 21% discount rate; 7% royalty) and multi-period excess earnings under the income approach ($90 million; 19% discount rate).

- Customer deposits and deferred revenue at consolidation: Recorded a $264 million customer deposit at fair value (discount rates 2.54%–3.23%), repayable 2029–2034 contingent on purchase obligations; and $1,070 million of deferred revenue at fair value using a cost build-up method with a normal profit margin.

- Impairment of long-lived assets: Process for identifying and measuring impairments, including indicators (market price declines, adverse changes in use/legal factors, cost overruns, sustained losses, early disposal). Asset groups are identified at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows, often combined across locations within segments sharing supply chains. Recoverability tests use undiscounted cash flows; if failed, fair value is estimated via an income approach. Assumptions are most sensitive to market growth, volume, and pricing.

- Precious metals in manufacturing equipment: Platinum and rhodium components are not depreciated due to long useful lives; reviewed for impairment across all stages (in-process, reclamation, fabrication). Carrying values were $3.5 billion (2021) and $3.4 billion (2020), both significantly below market value. Future impairment risk exists if Display Technologies or Specialty Materials experience significant demand/profitability declines.

- 2020 impairment charge: $217 million pre-tax impairment and disposal loss within “All Other” due to discontinuation/reprioritization of certain R&D programs; fair value measured with Level 3 inputs.

- Income taxes: Significant judgment in assessing realizability of deferred tax assets and evaluating uncertain tax positions under ASC 740 (more-likely-than-not threshold, recognition limited to amounts probable upon settlement). Estimates can change with new information.

- Fair value measurements: Use of observable and unobservable inputs under the fair value hierarchy and highest-and-best-use for non-financial assets. Major categories measured at fair value include investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives, valued primarily with observable market inputs.

- Derivatives and hedging: Interest rate swaps and FX forwards (yen, won, euro, TWD, yuan, pound). Cash flow hedge changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified when hedged items affect earnings; non-designated contracts recognized in earnings. Credit risk impacts deemed immaterial.

- Litigation and contingencies: Outcome assessments based on counsel, case law, and case-specific factors; other possible liabilities (e.g., tax planning, environmental) require judgment for accrual or disclosure; actual outcomes may require adjustments.

- Cross-references: Notes on investments, HSG transactions and acquisitions, restructuring/impairment, fair value measurements, and the Legal Proceedings section.

ess the recoverability of the carrying value of long-lived assets when an indicator of impairment has been identified. We review long-lived assets ineach quarter in which imp
airment indicators are present. We must exercise judgment in assessing whether an event of impairment has occurred.

e they have very low physical losses and are repeatedly reclaimed and reused in our manufacturing process over a very long useful life. Preciousmetals are reviewed

t held for trading or other non-manufacturing related purposes. 
Examples of events or

For purposes of recognition and me
asurement of an impairment loss, a long-lived asset or assets is grouped with other assets and liabilities at the lowest level for whichidentifiable cash f
lows are largely independent of the cash flows of other assets and liabilities. We must exercise judgment in assessing the lowest level for which identifiablecash flows are largely ind
ependent of the cash flows of other assets and liabilities. Our assessment is performed at the reportable segment level. For most of our reportablesegments, we concluded that lo
cations or businesses within these segments which share production along the supply chain must be combined to appropriately identify cashflows that are largely

For long-lived assets, when impai
rment indicators are present, we compare estimated undiscounted future cash flows, including the eventual disposition of the asset group atmarket value, to the ass
ets’ carrying value to determine if the asset group is recoverable. This assessment requires the exercise of judgment in assessing the future use of andprojected value to be de
rived from the assets to be held and used. Assessments also consider changes in asset utilization, including the temporary idling of capacity and theexpected timing for pl

re net cash flows, including the eventual disposition at market value of long-lived assets, and considers the fair market value of all precious metals, ifapplicable. We assess th
e recoverability of the carrying value of long-lived assets at the lowest level for which identifiable cash flows are largely independent of the cashflows of other asset
s and liabilities. If there is an impairment, a loss is recorded to reflect the difference between the assets’ fair value and carrying value. Our estimates arebased upon our historical expe
rience, our commercial relationships, and available external information about future trends. We believe fair value assessments are mostsensitive to market growth

title: Fair value measures
heading: Fair value measures
start_phrase: As required, Corning uses two kinds of inputs to de termine the fair value of assets and liabilities: observable and unobservable.
summary:
- References to related financial statement notes, including restructuring, impairment, and other charges (Note 2) and fair value measurements (Note 16).
- Income taxes: assessment of realizability of deferred tax assets requires forecasting future book/taxable income and evaluating tax planning strategies; recognition of uncertain tax positions under ASC 740 using a “more-likely-than-not” (>50%) threshold and measurement limited to amounts more than 50% likely to be realized; estimates may change with new information.
- Fair value measurements: use of observable and unobservable inputs organized into a three-level hierarchy; requirement to use observable market data when available and apply highest-and-best-use for non-financial assets; major items measured at fair value include short- and long-term investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives, typically valued via a market approach using quoted prices in active or less-active markets.
- Derivatives and hedging: instruments include interest rate swaps and foreign currency forwards (hedging exposures in JPY, KRW, EUR, TWD, CNY, GBP); cash flow hedges recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings when hedged items affect income; non-designated contracts marked to earnings; credit risk considered immaterial.
- Litigation: outcome assessments rely on legal counsel, case law, and case-specific factors; material matters referenced in Legal Proceedings.
- Other potential liabilities: judgments about inherently uncertain future events (e.g., tax planning and environmental matters) determine accruals or disclosures; actual outcomes may require adjustments.

Fair value measures
 
As required, Corning uses two kinds of inputs to de
termine the fair value of assets and liabilities: observable and unobservable. Observable inputs are based on market dataor independent sources, while unobse
rvable inputs are based on the Company’s own market assumptions. Once inputs have been characterized, we prioritize the inputs usedto measure fair valu
e into one of three broad levels. Characterization of fair value inputs is required for those accounting pronouncements that prescribe or permit fair valuemeasurement. In addit
ion, observable market data must be used when available and the highest-and-best-use measure should be applied to non-financial assets. Corning’smajor categories of financial as
sets and liabilities required to be measured at fair value are short-term and long-term investments, certain pension asset investments andderivatives. These cat
egories use observable inputs only and are measured using a market approach based on quoted prices in markets considered active or in markets inwhich there are few trans
actions. 
Derivative assets and li
abilities may include interest rate swaps and forward exchange contracts that are measured using observable quoted prices for similar assets andliabilities.  Includ
ed in our forward exchange contracts are foreign currency hedges that hedge our cash flow and translation exposure resulting from movements in theJapanese yen, South Korean won, euro, new Taiwan doll
ar, Chinese yuan and British pound.  Changes in the fair value of contracts designated as cash flow hedges arerecorded in accumula
ted other comprehensive loss in shareholders’ equity and reclassified into income when the underlying hedged item impacts earnings.  For contractsthat are not designated 
as accounting hedges, changes in fair value are recorded in earnings in the translated earnings contract gain (loss), net line of the consolidatedstatements of income.  
In arriving at the fair value of Corning’s derivative assets and liabilities, we have considered the appropriate valuation and risk criteria, including suchfactors as credit risk of t
he relevant party to the transaction.  Amounts related to credit risk are not material.

title: Revenue recognition
heading: Revenue recognition
start_phrase: The Company recognizes revenue when all performance obligations under the terms of a contract with our customer are satisfied, and control of the product has been transferred to the customer.
summary:
- Interest rate sensitivity at December 31, 2021: a 25 bps decrease in each spot rate would reduce shareholders’ equity by $137 million (pre-tax); a 25 bps increase would raise equity by $129 million.
- Nonlinearity note: impacts of changes greater than 25 bps are not proportional; analyses reflect changing one assumption at a time, and economic factors may affect multiple assumptions simultaneously.
- U.S. OPEB sensitivity table: a 25 bps decrease in each spot rate increases 2022 pre-tax OPEB expense by $2 million and APBO by $22 million; a 25 bps increase decreases 2022 pre-tax OPEB expense by $2 million and APBO by $20 million.
- Revenue recognition policy: revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied and control transfers to the customer; if customer acceptance clauses prevent objective determination of transfer of control, revenue is recognized upon acceptance and satisfaction of obligations.
- Most product sales do not contain multiple elements.
- Certain contracts recognize revenue over time, using either straight-line amortization or an input method based on incurred and forecasted costs aligned to satisfaction of performance obligations.
- New accounting standards: reference to Note 1 (Summary of Significant Accounting Policies) for details.
text:
Revenue recognition
 
The Company recognizes revenue when 
all performance obligations under the terms of a contract with our customer are satisfied, and control of the product has beentransferred to the customer.
 If customer acceptance clauses are present and it cannot be objectively determined that control has been transferred, revenue is only recordedwhen customer acceptanc
e is received and all performance obligations have been satisfied. Sales of goods typically do not include multiple product and/or service elements.Corning also has contractual 
arrangements with certain customers in which we recognize revenue over time. The performance obligations under these contracts generallyrequire services to be p
erformed over time, resulting in either a straight-line amortization method or an input method using incurred and forecasted expense to predictrevenue recognition pat
terns which follows satisfaction of the performance obligation.

summary:

Effects are non-linear for changes greater than 25 bps. For U.S. OPEB plans, a 25 bps decrease in each spot rate increases 2022 pre-tax OPEB expense by $2 million and APBO by $22 million; a 25 bps increase decreases expense by $2 million and APBO by $20 million. title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risks
heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risks
start_phrase: We operate and conduct busin ess in many foreign countries and as a result are exposed to movements in foreign currency exchange rates.
summary:
- The company operates globally and faces foreign currency exchange risk affecting both earnings from foreign-currency transactions and translation of foreign subsidiaries’ results.
- Primary currency exposures include the Japanese yen, South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar, Chinese yuan, and euro.
- It mitigates FX risk using OTC derivatives—primarily foreign exchange forwards and options—aligned with the timing of underlying commitments.
- Hedging programs include cash flow hedges (to protect cash flows from sales/purchases), net investment hedges (to protect investments in foreign operations), and undesignated hedges (to offset economic currency risks on monetary balances and earnings), with notable use of average rate forwards to protect translated earnings in Japanese yen.
- Counterparty credit risk is managed by transacting with a diversified set of highly rated financial institutions; no collateral is required by either party, and no losses from counterparty defaults are expected.
- Sensitivity analysis: a 10% adverse FX move at December 31, 2021 could reduce the fair value of open FX derivatives and foreign-denominated debt by $0.7 billion (vs. $1.0 billion at December 31, 2020); for the Japanese yen specifically, the potential loss is $0.6 billion in 2021 (vs. $0.8 billion in 2020). These derivative losses are expected to largely offset gains on the hedged items and transactions.
- Item 8 refers to audited Consolidated Financial Statements and related notes located in Part IV, Item 15 of the Form 10-K.
- Item 9 reports no changes in, or disagreements with, accountants on accounting and financial disclosure.

Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disc
losures About Market Risks 
We operate and conduct busin
ess in many foreign countries and as a result are exposed to movements in foreign currency exchange rates. Our exposure to exchange rateshas the following effects:
 
•
Exchange rate movements on financial instruments and transactions denominated in foreign currencies that impact earnings; and•
Exchange rate movements upon conversion of net assets and net income of foreign subsidiaries for which the functional currency is not the U.S. dollar. 
Our most significant fore
ign currency exposure relates to the Japanese yen, South Korean won, new Taiwan dollar, Chinese yuan, and the euro. We seek to mitigate theimpact of exchange ra
te movements in our income statement by using over-the-counter (OTC) derivative instruments including foreign exchange forward and optioncontracts. In general, 
these hedges expire coincident with the timing of the underlying foreign currency commitments and transactions. 
We are exposed to potenti
al losses in the event of non-performance by our counterparties to these derivative contracts. However, we minimize this risk by maintaining adiverse group of highly-rat
ed major financial institutions as our counterparties. We do not expect to record any losses as a result of such counterparty default. Neither we norour counterparties are require
d to post collateral for these financial instruments. 
Our cash flow hedging activiti
es utilize OTC foreign exchange forward contracts to reduce the risk that movements in exchange rates will adversely affect the net cash flowsresulting from the sal
e of products to foreign customers and purchases from foreign suppliers. In our net investment hedging activity, we use OTC foreign exchange forwardcontracts to hedge a port
ion of our net investment in certain foreign operations against movements in exchange rates. We also use OTC foreign exchange forward and optioncontracts that are no
t designated as hedged instruments. These contracts are used to offset economic currency risks. The undesignated hedges limit exposure to foreignfunctional currency f
luctuations related to certain subsidiaries’ monetary assets, monetary liabilities and net earnings in foreign currencies. A significant portion of theCompany’s non-U.S. revenue is denominated 
in Japanese yen. When this revenue is translated back to U.S. dollars, the Company is exposed to foreign exchange ratemovements in the Japanese y
en. To protect translated earnings against movements in the Japanese yen, the Company has entered into a series of average rate forwards andother derivative instruments.
 
We use a sensitivity ana
lysis to assess the market risk associated with foreign currency exposure. Market risk is defined as the potential change in fair value of assets andliabilities resul
ting from an adverse movement in foreign currency exchange rates. At December 31, 2021, with respect to open foreign exchange forward and optioncontracts, and foreign deno
minated debt with values exposed to exchange rate movements, a 10% adverse movement in quoted foreign currency exchange rates could resultin a loss in fair value of 
these instruments of $0.7 billion compared to $1.0 billion at December 31, 2020. Specific to the Japanese yen, a 10% adverse movement in quotedyen exchange rates could r
esult in a loss in fair value of these instruments of $0.6 billion and $0.8 billion at December 31, 2021 and 2020, respectively. The Companyexpects that these hypothe
tical losses from a 10% adverse movement in quoted foreign currency exchange rates on the derivative financial instruments should largely offsetgains on the assets, liabil
ities and future transactions being hedged.

summary:
- Item 9A: Controls and Procedures
  - Disclosure Controls and Procedures: The principal executive and financial officers evaluated Corning’s disclosure controls under Exchange Act Rules 13a-15/15d-15 and concluded they were effective as of the report period end.   - Internal Control Over Financial Reporting (ICFR):
    - Management’s responsibility: Establish and maintain adequate ICFR to provide reasonable assurance over reliable financial reporting and GAAP-compliant financial statements.

    - Limitations: ICFR has inherent limitations and effectiveness may change over time.
    - Evaluation framework: COSO Internal Control—Integrated Framework (2013).
    - Conclusion: ICFR was effective as of December 31, 2021. Effectiveness audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, independent registered public accounting firm.

start_phrase:
We have audited the ac
companying consolidated balance sheets of Corning Incorporated and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2021 and 2020,
summary:
- Independent auditor’s report from PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP to Corning Incorporated’s board and shareholders.
- Unqualified opinions: (1) consolidated financial statements present fairly in conformity with U.S. GAAP for the years ended 2019–2021 and as of December 31, 2021 and 2020; (2) effective internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of December 31, 2021, based on COSO 2013.
- Basis for opinions: management’s and auditor’s responsibilities, PCAOB standards, independence, audit scope and procedures (risk assessment, testing, evaluation of accounting principles, estimates, presentation; ICFR understanding, testing, and evaluation), and acknowledgment of ICFR limitations.
- Critical Audit Matter: Income taxes—receivables related to South Korean tax disputes (tax years 2010–2018). Company must deposit disputed taxes; management recorded a $350 million non-current receivable based on a more-likely-than-not assessment of prevailing on appeal. CAM involved significant judgment, required specialized tax expertise, control testing, and evaluation of the likelihood the positions will be sustained.
- Auditor details: PwC New York; report dated February 14, 2022; auditor of the Company since 1944.
- Consolidated Statements of Income (2019–2021) highlights:
  - 2021: Net sales $14.082B; cost of sales $9.019B; gross margin $5.063B; operating expenses (SG&A $1.827B; R&D&E $0.995B; amortization $0.129B); operating income $2.112B.
  - Other items: equity in earnings of affiliates $35M; interest income $11M; interest expense $(300)M; translated earnings contract gain $354M; other income (expense), net $185M; no transaction-related gain in 2021 (2019 included $498M).
  - Income before taxes $2.397B; provision for income taxes $(491)M; net income attributable to Corning $1.906B.
  - EPS 2021: basic $1.30; diluted $1.28.
- Reconciliation to net income available to common shareholders: deductions for Series A convertible preferred dividends ($24M in 2021) and $803M excess consideration for preferred stock redemption; resulting 2021 net income available to common shareholders $1.079B. References to Notes 17 and 18 for details.

Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm 
 
To the
 Board of Directors and Shareholders of Corning Incorporated 
Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
We have audited the ac
companying consolidated balance sheets of Corning Incorporated and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2021 and 2020, and therelated consolidated s
tatements of income, comprehensive income, changes in shareholders’ equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December31, 2021, inclu
ding the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”). We also have audited the Company's internal control over financialreporting as of December 31, 2021, b
ased on criteria established in Internal Control - Integrated Framework  (2013) issued by the Committee o f Sponsoring Organizations ofthe Treadway Commission (COSO). 
In our opinion, the consolidated
 financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of the Company as of December 31, 2021and 2020
, and the results of its operations and its cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2021 in conformity with accounting principlesgenerally accepted 
in the United States of America. Also in our opinion, the Company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reportingas of December 31, 2021, based on cri
teria established in Internal Control - Integrated Framework  (2013) issued by the COSO. Basis for Opinions
The Company's management is respons
ible for these consolidated financial statements, for maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting, and for itsassessment of the effe
ctiveness of internal control over financial reporting, included in Management's Annual Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting appearingunder Item 9A. Our responsibility 
is to express opinions on the Company’s consolidated financial statements and on the Company's internal control over financial reportingbased on our audits. We are a pub
lic accounting firm registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States) (PCAOB) and are required to beindependent with respect to 
the Company in accordance with the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and ExchangeCommission and the PCAOB.
We conducted our audits in a
ccordance with the standards of the PCAOB. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audits to obtain reasonable assurance aboutwhether the consolidate
d financial statements are free of material misstatement, whether due to error or fraud, and whether effective internal control over financial reportingwas maintained in all m
aterial respects. Our audits of the consolidated
 financial statements included performing procedures to assess the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,whether due to error or fr
aud, and performing procedures that respond to those risks. Such procedures included examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amountsand disclosures in the consolid
ated financial statements. Our audits also included evaluating the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management,as well as evaluating the ov
erall presentation of the consolidated financial statements. Our audit of internal control over financial reporting included obtaining anunderstanding of internal 
control over financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectivenessof internal control bas
ed on the assessed risk. Our audits also included performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances. We believe thatour audits provide a reasonab
le basis for our opinions.Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Repor
tingA company’s internal contro
l over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparationof financial state
ments for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal control over financial reporting includesthose policies and pr
ocedures that (i) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of theassets of the company;
 (ii) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generallyaccepted accounting pr
inciples, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of thecompany; and (iii) provid
e reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that couldhave a material effect on the fina
ncial statements.63
Table of Contents 
Because of its inherent l
imitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness tofuture periods are subje
ct to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or proceduresmay deteriorate.
Critical Audit Matter
The critical audit matter communicated
 below is a matter arising from the current period audit of the consolidated financial statements that was communicated or required tobe communicated to the au
dit committee and that (i) relates to accounts or disclosures that are material to the consolidated financial statements and (ii) involved ourespecially challeng
ing, subjective, or complex judgments. The communication of critical audit matters does not alter in any way our opinion on the consolidated financialstatements, taken as a whol
e, and we are not, by communicating the critical audit matter below, providing a separate opinion on the critical audit matter or on the accounts ordisclosures to which it rel
ates.Income Taxes - Receivables for Sou
th Korean Tax DisputesAs described in Notes 1, 8, and 11 to the consol
idated financial statements, in evaluating the tax benefits associated with the Company’s various tax filing positions,management records a 
tax benefit for uncertain tax positions using the highest cumulative tax benefit that is more likely than not to be realized. Adjustments are made to theasset or liability fo
r unrecognized tax benefits in the period in which the Company files the return containing the tax position or when new information becomes available.The Company is currently appea
ling certain South Korean tax assessments and tax refund claims for tax years 2010 through 2018. The Company is required to deposit thedisputed tax amounts with the South Kore
an government as a condition of its appeal of any tax assessments. The Company believes that it is more likely than not that theCompany will prevail in the app
eal process and as a result, management recorded a non-current receivable of $350 million as of December 31, 2021.The principal consideratio
ns for our determination that performing procedures relating to the receivables for South Korean tax disputes is a critical audit matter are (i) thesignificant judgment by m
anagement when applying the more likely than not recognition criteria to the Company’s uncertain tax positions based on the application of the taxlaw; (ii) a high degree o
f auditor judgment, subjectivity, and effort in performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence relating to management’s assumption that theCompany will prevail in the app
eal of any tax assessments; and (iii) the audit effort involved the use of professionals with specialized skill and knowledge.Addressing the matter involv
ed performing procedures and evaluating audit evidence in connection with forming our overall opinion on the consolidated financialstatements. These procedu
res included testing the effectiveness of controls relating to uncertain tax positions, including management’s assessment of the South Korean taxdisputes. These procedures also

title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies - Introduction
heading: 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
summary: This section outlines Corning Incorporated’s significant accounting policies, covering consolidation under U.S. GAAP (majority-owned entities consolidated; equity method for 20%–50% interests; fair value or cost-minus-impairment for other investments), and a 2020 transaction in which HSG redeemed DuPont’s $250 million interest, resulting in Corning owning 100% of HS LLC and 80.5% of HSO LLC (HSG consolidated in “All Other”). It details extensive use of estimates (revenue, restructuring, impairments, valuations, environmental/legal liabilities, taxes, pensions, share-based pay), revenue recognition primarily at a point in time with allowances, warranties, and some over-time service arrangements, and R&D expensed as incurred ($0.8B, $1.0B, $0.8B in 2021–2019). Foreign currency policies identify local functional currencies (notably a Taiwanese subsidiary using JPY), with a $126M net translation gain in 2021 and net transaction losses of $37M and $19M in 2020 and 2019; translation effects are in AOCI. Share-based compensation is measured at grant-date fair value via a multiple-point Black-Scholes model; cash equivalents are highly liquid investments maturing in three months or less; supplemental cash flow data include capex accruals of $357M/$231M/$592M and cash paid for interest $287M/$298M/$248M (including capitalized interest $36M/$58M/$54M) and income taxes $377M/$220M/$474M for 2021–2019. Additional policies address the allowance for doubtful accounts, environmental liabilities (probable and estimable, with insurance receivables when virtually certain), inventories at lower of cost or NRV (FIFO), PP&E lives (buildings 10–40 years; equipment 2–20; e.g., computer hardware/software 3–7, manufacturing 2–15) with precious metals not depreciated but depleted, lease accounting for operating/finance ROU assets and liabilities, impairment testing using undiscounted cash flows and income approach fair values (including precious metals), employee retirement plan cost recognition (including corridor-based mark-to-market), and income taxes (asset-liability method, uncertain tax positions, and indefinite reinvestment of certain foreign earnings).

Summary of Significant Accounting Policies 
Organization
 
Corning Incorporated is a provid
er of high-performance glass for notebook computers, flat panel desktop monitors, display televisions, and other information displayapplications; carr
ier network and enterprise network products for the telecommunications industry; ceramic substrates for gasoline and diesel engines in automotive andheavy-duty vehicle mark
ets; laboratory products for the scientific community and specialized polymer products for biotechnology applications; advanced optical materialsfor the semiconductor indus
try and the scientific community; polycrystalline silicon products and other technologies. In these notes, the terms “Corning,” “Company,” “we,”“us,” or “our” mean Corning Inco
rporated and subsidiary companies. 
Basis of Presentation and Principles of Consolidation
 
Corning’s consolidated financ
ial statements were prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles in the U.S. and include the assets, liabilities, revenueand expenses of all major
ity-owned subsidiaries over which Corning exercises control. 
The equity method of account
ing is used for investments in affiliated companies that are not  controlled by Corning and in which our interest is generally between 20% and50% and we have significant in
fluence over the entity. Our share of earnings or losses of these affiliated companies is included in consolidated operating results. 
For our investments in compani
es that we do not  control and for which we do not  have the ability to exercise significant influence over operating and financial policies, weuse the fair value method
 to account for the investments if readily determinable fair values are available. For the investments without readily determinable fair values, wemeasure them at cost 
minus impairment, if any, plus or minus changes resulting from observable price changes in orderly transactions for the identical or a similarinvestment.
 
On 
September 9, 2020, HSG redeemed the entire ownership  interest of DuPont in HSG with a value of $250 million.  Upon completion of the Redemption, the Companyobtained a 100% interest 
in HS LLC and an 80.5% interest in HSO LLC, which are affiliated entities within HSG.  HSG's results have been consolidated in “All Other”. Refer to Note 
3  (Investments) and Note 4  (HSG Transactions and Acquisitions) to the consolidated financial statements for more information. 
All intercompany accounts, 
transactions and profits are eliminated in consolidation. 
Certain prior year amount
s have been reclassified to conform to the current year’s presentation. These reclassifications had no  impact on the results of operations, financialposition, or changes in sharehold
ers’ equity. 
Use of Estimates
 
The preparation of finan
cial statements, in conformity with GAAP, requires management to make estimates and assumptions affecting reported amounts of assets, liabilities,revenue, expenses and the disc
losure of contingent assets and liabilities in the consolidated financial statements and related notes. Significant estimates and assumptions inthese consolidated finan
cial statements include estimates associated with revenue recognition, restructuring charges, goodwill and long-lived asset impairment tests,estimates of acquired assets
 and liabilities, estimates of fair value of investments, equity interests, environmental and legal liabilities, income taxes and deferred tax valuationallowances, assumptions used in c
alculating pension and other postretirement employee benefit expenses and the fair value of share-based compensation. Due to the inherentuncertainty involved in m
aking estimates, actual results reported in future periods may  be different from these estimates. 
70
